utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and joined by our intern, Rodolphe Genissel, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Aleksandar Aleksic for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin with the witness who is scheduled today, there are a number of matters which the Chamber would raise. The first is that to settle the matter of the UN holiday which intervenes shortly after the scheduled beginning of the resumption of this case, we confirm that we will reconvene on the 31st of August, instead of the 29th. The second matter is that the sitting arrangements that have been confirmed has confirmed e-mails that the Stanisic and Zupljanin case will sit in sets of two weeks from Monday of the first week to the Friday of the one following. Accordingly, in the week when the court reconvenes on the 31st of August, it will adjourn for two weeks and all other factors remain unchanged. That is, it will reconvene on the 9th of September. The Zupljanin Defence, we expect, would start its case when the Chamber reconvenes on the 31st of August, and, accordingly, the Zupljanin Defence is to provide its list of witnesses in the order that they will be called by the 8th of July, which is the end of this week. Yesterday, there was filed a motion by the Stanisic Defence for leave to amend its Rule 65 exhibit list, and we would request the Prosecution urgently respond to that. As you would be aware from reading it, the motion seeks the addition of two documents both of which were disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution, and the Prosection itself intends to use one of the documents with the witness who is next on the stand. Mr. Hannis, could we inquire as to whether you are able to respond immediately or whether we could expect to hear from you at the close of business today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was on my list to tell you this morning that the Prosecution has no objection to the addition of those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So noted. Could we go into private session for the other two matters, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, before you begin, Mr. Hannis, I'm reminded that having regard to what the -- you said earlier that we should formally grant the motion of the Stanisic Defence to amend its Rule 65 list. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You mostly answered the questions I had on my list to raise this morning. But I just wanted to clarify your ruling. As I understand it then, after the recess, the first time we will be sitting will be on 31st of August, that's the Wednesday after the Tuesday UN holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We would sit then for the remaining three days that week and five days the following week, and that is through September 9th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You understand us correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then am I correct then for the next two weeks you and Judge Delvoie would be in Haradinaj, and we would return to this case on the 26th of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, as we understand it, the previously announced two week/two week pattern would then pick up. So whatever your calendar tells you, that would be correct. Of course, to state the obvious, once this pattern begins, we would see whether for purely practical reasons it has to be varied, but that's how we start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The other matter is you have directed the Zupljanin Defence to file by the end of this week the -- their batting order for their witnesses. We would ask that they also indicate or confirm the mode of testimony for those witness. That is, the ones that have previously been listed as viva voce to inform us whether or not they're still viva voce, there's no request to change any of the proposed modes of testimony. And I believe that was the last thing I needed to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we go back in a private session for just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, I must respectively remind the Chamber that there are still three pending motions from -- from Stanisic Defence, and those are two -- two motions for amendments to 65 ter of 6th of May and 3rd of June, and the admission of expert report and the -- and the footnotes filed on the 23rd of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You needn't feel embarrassed about that reminder, Mr. Zecevic. The Chamber, of course, is alive to the fact that these motions are outstanding and that you couldn't formally close your case until they are resolved. But we will tell you that they are well in hand which is an explanation that you would have heard before. I can say nothing further. The Chamber certainly hasn't forgotten them. But as I said, you needn't feel embarrassed in terms of the exercise of your own duty to so remind the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if there is nothing else that need delay us, could the usher please escort the witness in. While the witness is on his way in, I know I have this written down somewhere but could the parties indicate to me the times that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Zecevic originally indicated 20 hours for direct examination. I had not indicated a time. I thought something in the neighbourhood of 12 to 16 hours. When I got the proofing note this morning, seeing the eight very broad somewhat vague topics, I guess I want to say 20 hours to be on the safe side. I'm confident it will be less than that. But given what is in the proofing note, I have some concerns that I may need more time than I originally anticipated. And I don't know for the Zupljanin Defence if they have an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend Mr. Krgovic will examine this witness. Just to be on the safe side, I will state my estimate of two hours. We may, after all, refrain from examining this witness all together. But to be safe, I'll say two hours for D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. Sir, will you please read the solemn declaration on the card that the usher is now handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And from your responses so far, I take it that you are hearing me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would begin by pointing out to you that the solemn declaration that you have just taken imposes upon you an obligation to speak the truth, and not to mislead the Trial Chamber. This Chamber is, as a part of the Tribunal, set up under the Statute which sets it up -- is empowered to impose sanctions for giving misleading or false testimony before the Chamber. So that is a reminder that I would give you at the beginning of each session -- of each day's sitting of the solemn declaration that you have taken and the obligations it imposes upon you. I would begin by welcoming you to the Chamber -- to the Tribunal and agreeing to appear as a witness. And the first question I have is whether you have previously given testimony before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in any of the territories that comprise the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I will come back to explain to you briefly the procedure so that you have an understanding as to how we -- how your evidence will be led. But would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goran Macar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your profession, or what was your profession, and what is your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on 14th November, 1954, in Sokolac, Sokolac municipality, Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm an economist by training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian. An Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been called as a witness by the Defence of Mr. Stanisic, and council representing Mr. Stanisic will begin by asking you questions. When he is through, counsel for Mr. Stanisic's co-accused, Mr. Zupljanin may, as you may have heard as you were walking into the courtroom, himself opt to ask questions of you. That remains to be seen. After counsel for Mr. Zupljanin, then counsel to your left, who represents the Prosecution, would have a right to cross-examine. And then counsel calling you would have a right to re-examine in matters which -- on which they wish clarification arising out of your testimony, out of your cross-examination. The Judges who comprise the Trial Chamber may at that point or indeed at any earlier point themselves have questions of you. In terms of the time that this exercise will take, counsel calling you have indicated that your testimony is expected to run over a period of 20 hours. Counsel for the Prosecution has indicated a like period of time, so a total of 40 hours. And Mr. Aleksic, on behalf of the Zupljanin Defence, has said that if they have any questions it is unlikely to exceeds two hours. The Court sits either in morning or afternoon sessions because with the limited courtroom space, we must make the courtroom available for other trials. And I believe we are scheduled to sit in morning sittings for the entirety of this week. Those periods of time that I have given you are broken up according to each day's sitting, which, for the morning would begin at 9.00 and end at 1.45, are broken up in periods of not more than an hour and a half, for the technical reasons that the proceedings of the Tribunal are recorded and the tapes have to be changed at those intervals. That allows for the convenience of yourself, counsel, and everyone else concerned to have breaks during the course of the day's sitting, that is, between the 9.00 to 1.45 day that comprises the period that the Court would sit. And -- but if for any reason you are distresses and need a break before the scheduled time, you would indicate that to us and we would certainly accommodate you. So unless you have any other questions by way -- that I can clarify for you, I would invite Mr. Zecevic, who appears as lead counsel ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- before -- I would invite Mr. Zecevic, who is lead counsel for Mr. Stanisic, to begin his cross-examination [sic]. But before he does, the Chamber requires and Mr. Zecevic would have communicated this to you, and I -- I'm going to invite him and perhaps we should go into private session briefly before his examination begins. Could we do that now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, tell me something about your professional background. When did you first get a job with the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: After obtaining my BA in economics in 1977, I started working on the 6th of June, 1977, with the city secretariat of the interior of the Ministry of the Interior of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I worked in the white-collar crime unit as an inspector. I remained in that unit until 1982 when I moved on to work as chief of the crime unit in the secretariat of the interior, the municipal secretariat of the interior in Sarajevo's Centar municipality. Centar. I remained in that position until 1987, which was when I went back to Sarajevo's SUP, secretariat of the interior of the city of Sarajevo, and I was back working with white collar crime. I worked as an inspector there until 1990. At that point in time, I was appointed head of general crime unit with the crime police of the city secretariat of the interior. In 1992, I started working as a co-ordinator with the crime police directorate of the Ministry of the Interior of the RS. I was then appointed chief of that directorate, and I remained in that position until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You say that you went back to Sarajevo city SUP in 1990. How long did you work there for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I stayed with Sarajevo's SUP as chief of the general crime unit between 1990 and the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start work with the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I started working with the Ministry of the Interior in the second half of April, after the 19th of April, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, when did you first meet Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I first met Mico Stanisic late in 1977, I believe, possibly early 1978. I was doing a SAJ in his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the period between 1990 and 1992, you said you worked with Sarajevo's SUP, S-U-P; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The national parties emerged as victorious in the 1990 elections. Did that change anything about the way the Ministry of the Interior operated, and if so, what exactly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: After the victory of the national parties, all the politics in Bosnia and Herzegovina changed and obviously that reflected on the work of the Ministry of the Interior. First, there was a peaceful lustration of the personnel working there from the municipal level all the way to the top of the MUP. Many of the people working at the time took an early retirement under the laws that then applied and some moved on to other jobs in the Ministry of the Interior. Obviously that had an immediate effect on the quality of the work being performed by the ministry. Late in 1991 and early 1992, the impact of these national parties on the way the Ministry of the Interior operated became very obvious. The ministry started breaking up at the seams along national lines or ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was a lustration effort in progress. Can you please explain what you mean. A quiet purge.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: There were experienced professionals working there, probably pursuing cases at the time against certain categories of persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about this term that you used, the purge. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: That means certain people in leading positions were removed from these leading positions in the Ministry of the Interior. And this all started with public security stations, the leading people there, and then went all the way up to the very top of the Ministry of the Interior. People were removed from their positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, what sort of a HR policy or personnel policy did you have in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, let me point out the following: Early in 1991, sometime in March, there was a census in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Members of the Ministry of the Interior of both the public security and the state security following the census had information indicating that the leaders of the party of democratic action, along with certain people in leading positions who were ethnic Muslims from the public security stations and the very top level of the MUP, had amplified the results of the census, during the census and after the census, representative of there being more people than there actually were. They included many of the citizens from the Sandzak area. This is an area straddling the border between the south of Serbia and the north of Montenegro, ethnic Muslims living there, and also some in Kosovo, a small portion of those. This information was available to the public security services and the State Security Services. I don't think the census was ever verified. Information was just passed along like that, passed on to the Ministry of the Interior. I am not aware that anyone from the ministry ever responded to those data or, indeed, that data was ever checked. Doubts persist about the results of the census. The Muslim part of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to avoid being registered all together, and they wanted all the parameters from the 1991 census to simply be adopted for the new round. The Party of Democratic Action, after this last census, asked for the results of the census and the relevant proportions to be applied to the work and the manning and personal policies in the Ministry of the Interior as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take this one step at a time, sir. Mr. Macar, first of all, I have to ask you to slow down a little. All of your evidence is being interpreted, which is no simple task at all, given the fact that we are using a lot of data here. Based on such information as was available to you regarding the alleged blowing up of the numbers of Muslims from the Sandzak territory, and then adding those numbers to the census lists in Bosnia and Herzegovina, can you please tell me this: Did Sandzak belong to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No. The Sandzak area straddled the border between south Serbia and north Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you could tell, what was the ethnic makeup of the Sandzak area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: There was a Muslim majority there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that was available to you in 1991 regarding the numbers being boosted, the census numbers, I'm talking about the 1991 census, of course, do you remember what the discrepancy was, what the differential was between the real numbers and the boosted numbers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to check the numbers in my superior's office. The numbers would have been about 300.000 or 310.000 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned your superior. Who are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Jozo Leutar, chief of the crime police sector in the secretariat of the interior of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: He was an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, how many citizens did it number, roughly speaking, at the time of the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: About 4 million, several 100.000s. Maybe 300.000 or 400.000, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was the general principle that applied to hire people along ethnic lines in order to have some sort of an ethnic balance within the service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: In the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, we tried to achieve some sort of ethnic equality in terms of the numbers of people being hired and that applied to the Ministry of the Interior, too. At the time in the Ministry of the Interior, there were maybe slightly over 40 per cent Serbs working there. It is all about the people who applied for these jobs. The Serbs tended to apply more for the uniformed jobs, and that is why the quality was slightly disrupted there, as far as the uniformed jobs were concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please pause each time after I ask you a question so that the interpreters can hear your answer and also one step at a time. The 40 per cent Serbs, which segment of the Ministry of the Interior is that in reference to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The police, the uniformed police on the beat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to my original question: What was the personnel policy following the census in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Following the census, the Party for Democratic Action, in particular, tried to have this parity principle established in line with the results of the census. Nevertheless, this equality, in terms of equal numbers, was not what it should have been, especially within the police, and I'm talking about the city of Sarajevo. In the public security stations, you had reserve police forces. And in most municipalities the balance was disrupted and there were far more Muslims being hired as reserve policemen. One thing that is particularly noteworthy is this: Many of the Muslim citizens from Sandzak were being taken on as reserve policemen at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the citizens who arrived from the Sandzak territory? Did they have the republican citizenship of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No they didn't. They were either citizens of Serbia or Montenegro. And if I may just point out something else. Already back as far as 1990 and early 1991, there was a large-scale influx of people, ethnic Muslims from Sandzak and Albanians from Kosovo. Over that period, they took over the black market economy across the city of Sarajevo. They started exchanging foreign currency out in the street. They became dealers of foreign currency. There wasn't a single neighbourhood in Sarajevo where these people weren't operating. Dozens and dozens of them literally selling money. And they pursued all different kinds and forms of illicit trade in the city's markets, cigarettes, alcohol, food products, chemical products, that sort of thing. The police assessment and the assessment of the inspectors was that in 1991, late in 1990 and in 1991, over the several hundreds of millions of euros were missing from the state budget of Bosnia-Herzegovina because of this illicit trade. We tried to take a more organised approach in terms of fighting these types of crime. In 1991, we had several police operations involving large police numbers, and the operations were planned by the very leadership of the police. The principle being to gather as much information as possible -- to keep the information from leaking out. Most of the operations failed because information leaked all the time. Several hundred policemen were involved in these operations. We were trying to fight this type of crime that was rife across the city. I spoke to Mr. Leutar about the Muslim men involved with us in the planning and carrying out of these operations, and it appeared at one point that they were the source of these leaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, there's one thing we should clarify: Was it possible under the then-laws and regulations for citizens of another republic to be -- to become members of the reserve police force in a republic whose citizens they were not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The basic condition for somebody to be a member of the reserve force was to have a permanent residence and to go through a vetting process. They had to be checked in -- whether they had a police file and so on. And citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina only should have become members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a condition -- was one of the conditions that they have a permanent employment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: That was one of the criteria. It was not a criterion that could preclude anybody from becoming a member of the reserve force, but it -- that was something that was considered too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the checks in criminal records and police files for people who wanted to join the police force. Were any other categories of persons hired by the police during that period; and, if so, who?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I can say that it was observed that people with a shady past had been hired by the police, that some members of the reserve force had committed crimes, although it was a strict rule that perpetrators of crimes cannot become members of the reserve force. That was especially pronounced in the municipalities of Stari Grad and Centar, and I would like to add the following, speaking about the reserve force: In the Centar municipality, a huge number of reserve police officers was employed, exceeding all reasonable criteria, so that, in my street, for example, the citizens were wondering where are all these reserve police forces had all come from. They were all from Sandzak because you could easily tell by their accent so that my street was colloquially called Little Novi Pazar, and they were walking the streets armed, even with long-barrelled weapons, and I didn't know at the time why that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "my street," I didn't quite understand whether you lived there or ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I lived in Sarajevo, in down-town Sarajevo, the Vanja Racica [phoen] street, and the municipal secretariat was two metres from my courtyard. It was a small street, and it was easy to observe who entered the station, who exited, and who gathered round it. The building itself was close to the government building of Bosnia-Herzegovina where my late wife worked, and a school and kindergarten to which our children went were also nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that situation create any problems for some public security stations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: In late 1991 and early 1992, there was an escalation of disobeying the Law on Internal Affairs, especially in the Stari Grad municipality. The municipal leadership hired a huge number of Muslim citizens for the reserve force and reduced the number of stations where Serbs were reserve police officers. They also replaced the leadership. Where Serbs were commanders, they were replaced overnight by Muslims. Let me add that especially at the Stari Grad police station, it was a daily occurrence that some criminals were more often received by the police leadership than police staff, especially Serbs who needed to communicate with their superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This police station of Stari Grad, or the municipal secretariat of Stari Grad, if you will, is that a municipality that belongs to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The population was predominantly Muslim. And the adjacent municipalities were Pale and Centar. If I may continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The way the leadership of the reserve force was replaced, and I'm referring to Serbs, since the police force had long-barrelled weapons, the -- these weapons were taken away from them. In the reserve police stations where most of the police officers were Serbs, the commanders of those reserve stations were replaced by Muslims, and the weapons were taken to the secretariat of internal affairs and redistributed to stations where the Muslims were the majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this situation resolved in the Stari Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I'd have to add, if I may, that in the Stari Grad municipality, criminals came to see the police leadership daily. Open threats had already been issued to police officers of Serbian ethnicity, not only by criminals but also by some police officers from that station. In the process of assigning regular tasks, Serb police officers would mostly get marginal tasks, although, until the end of 1991, they had their respective areas where they worked. Muslims were assigned to work there instead. When members of paramilitary Muslim formations began to come and see the police leadership regularly, the Serbian police officers wrote an open letter in which they listed the problems they were facing. They requested that these problems be resolved. However, the MUP headquarters, more specifically the police administration, did nothing to take measures to improve the situation and the -- and sanction the officers who had been at the root of the problem. It was agreed that some Serbian police officers be transferred to other public security stations. Four inspectors then joined my department, and they were to stay there until the situation at the Stari Grad station changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] let us see 1D132, please. I have this binder for the witness. If the usher could please hand it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please approach the microphones so you can be heard better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 3, please, in your binder. But let us wait for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there no English available?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document, and we read that it was drafted by the staff of Serb ethnicity in the Stari Grad public security station, and this document was sent to the Ministry of the Interior, the Sarajevo Security Services Centre, and the Sarajevo Secretariat of the Interior. Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I know this document. The police officers at Stari Grad who were Serbs outlined the problems they were facing in 1991 and 1992. Right at the beginning, I remember these comments, especially because four officers were transferred to the SUP of the city of Sarajevo. They say that members of the Green Berets were in communication with the leadership and the leadership of the SDA, and let me explain. The MUP and the public security services, as well as the State Security Service, as soon as May 1991, got information that the SDA party was establishing paramilitary units called the Patriotic League, or Green Berets, respectively. The officers of my department found out, in the course of their operative work, that some criminals from Sarajevo were recruited by the Green Berets, and some of them even became commanders of those units. Let me mention some of these criminals: Juka Prazina, a well-known criminal who had been convicted to serve prison sentences; Ismet Bajramovic, also known as Celo, who had been convicted for the most serious crimes such as plotting to murder somebody and robbery and so on. He was convicted to serve -- he was sentenced to ten years in prison and was to serve in Lepoglava, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me just ask you to slow down once more because the interpreter failed to understand what you are trying to say. Whose murder was Ismet Bajramovic, also known as Celo, preparing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The murder of the Sarajevo prosecutor who was in charge of the case against Bajramovic and his group. They were committing crimes, robbery and theft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did these persons have any official documents?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I know that Ismet Bajramovic, Celo, had a BH MUP ID.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information indicating that candidates were sent for training to the MUP of the Republic of Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was sometime in the summer of 1991. We received information indicating that the Party of Democratic Action was sending ethnic Muslims to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb to be trained there. We believed that this was quite revealing. This was a political party sending people to be trained as police officers elsewhere; whereas, we, in Sarajevo, had a specialised training centre where the police were trained. They had a secondary school for police officers where courses were organised for new police officers for forensic experts and crime -- future crime squad officers. We, among the topmost police ranks, commented on these policies, and I think Leutar actually wrote up some documents to that effect. Nevertheless, as far as the HQ was concerned, I'm not sure whether anyone continued or indeed performed any checks in order to find out about the real intentions of the people behind this operation. We even had some individual Muslim citizens who came to ask questions about this. They had heard that people were being sent to Zagreb for training. They wondered how this could be done because they thought the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina was behind this operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your information, was the Ministry of the Interior involved in that operation, or was this something that was being done by the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: You had the leaders of the SDA, on the one hand, and the MUP's Muslims on the other. There were strong links between the two, so I should imagine that they were somehow involved in that as well, simply because no one organised any activities whatsoever to check that information and to check the background to everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. From a security aspect, how would you characterise the situation in Sarajevo, since that was where you worked? I'm talking about late 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The security situation was highly complex. Ethnic tensions were high. There was the Ministry of the Interior being broken up along ethnic lines. There were lots of deviations from the police norm, such as Stari Grad municipality which is an example that I mentioned and that I would like to say more about because it is also in relation to this issue. Many of the perpetrators of crimes whom arrest warrants were out, be it because they were suspected of committing a crime, or because court orders had been issued for these people to be caught and sentenced and punished, walked around Stari Grad municipality freely or even went to the secretariat of Stari Grad municipality, particularly to see Ismet Dahic and Mr. Bezdrop. One of the names is Enko Sakic. He was a commander of the Green Berets, specifically in Bistrik which is part of Stari Grad. He would see Mr. Dahic on a daily basis. In practical terms, people from my unit would keep them informed, and we kept telling them that there was an arrest warrant out on this person and that he had been sentenced and should serve his term. Nevertheless, no one ever even tried to arrest this person and to put him in prison, and the same state of disorder applied to more or less all of the policing there. Caco, a known criminal, who was a deputy commander of the Green Berets, would also go and see Mr. Dahic on a daily basis and the other Muslims in leading positions in that municipality. The municipal bodies did less and less in order to combat crime. On the other hand, crime, especially general crime, was on the rise. Sometime in September 1991, we took some steps against a group that was breaking into peoples' flats and houses in the broader Sarajevo area. During that operation, we arrested Caco, his brother, Suro [phoen] and other members of his family who were later arrested for the murder of the son of Avdo Hebib. We filed a criminal report against these people. One thing that is particularly noteworthy: During the interview that was conducted with this person, he told us that the deputy commander of the Green Berets for Bistrik, that he was the deputy commander, the deputy of Emir Sakic [phoen]. This was a company, there were armed men there. They had their own communications equipment. But this was an open secret. Everybody in Stari Grad knew about this, and, to some extent, in Sarajevo, too. There were links between the ethnic Muslims within the police force and these groups operating outside the system, and these links were open an obvious which certainly affected the way the police operated. That's why this letter was written by the police and the crime inspectors of Serb ethnicity from Stari Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphones and could we please lower the microphones so that the witness can actually speak into them. Thank you very much. The interpreters are really having a hard time hearing the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, given the situation that you just described, and given the malfunctioning, if I may call it that, of the Ministry of the Interior, did the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina do anything about it; if so, what exactly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The leaders of the Ministry of the Interior within the HQ and most of the municipal bodies did nothing. There were some individual cases -- I can talk about my line of work. We tried to act on any information or tip-offs that we received. For example, we received information indicating that there was something going on at the Konjic factory, that ammunition was being sent from the factory to Hrasnica, Ilidza and Novi Grad. Members of Patriotic League and the Green Berets were working together with these Konjic-based organisations and with the leaders of the Party of Democratic Action. We had information indicating that lorries were being escorted by the Muslim police members from Hadzici, specifically the deputy commander of that particular police unit who was also an ethnic Muslim, in the village of Drozgometva, or something like that, which is near Hadzici. We tried to mount an operation to monitor these activities but, at this point in time, we tried to take account of the fact that there could be information leaks. We tried to prevent that from happening because it had happened before. I was involved in this operation. Nevertheless, one of these lorries of the -- passed our car, we were on a stakeout, and they got as far as Novi Grad but we couldn't identify the location. My inspector and I drove straight to the home of this deputy commander. I can't remember his name. He was an elderly police officer, gaunt and tall. I called on him. His wife answered the door. I said I needed to speak to her husband for professional reasons. When he saw us he was quite unsettled, even scared. We shared a cup of coffee. I told him that we knew what he was up to, and said that he would be facing an arrest soon. Our operation had failed. But I had information, recent information indicating that this person specifically had given up escorting those convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to focus on the question that I actually asked you. The situation as you have just described, and please just provide brief answers, did you discuss this particular situation with any of your men in the leading positions in Sarajevo city SUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to my own superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your superior? What was his position or his view regarding the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: He believed that because the Ministry of the Interior wasn't operating properly and wasn't doing enough, the situation would becoming more and more complex every day. The hands of the police were tied, as it was, because there was no co-ordination between the ministry in the Security Services Centre of the SUP of the city itself and the public security stations and because of the direct influence in some segments of the ministry's HQ and the public security stations along ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient point to the take the break, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you told us about the situation in Sarajevo. What about the remaining territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? What was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I would like some more foundation about how this witness would know about the rest of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would also like to put on the record my objection to the nature of -- much of this is in the nature of tu quoque, and, therefore, I think it's irrelevant. I would like to have a standing objection in that regard so I don't have to keep getting up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm just trying to show the context of the events and the knowledge of the witness concerning the contents and how he understood the situation to be, and it doesn't -- it doesn't have to -- it's not tu quoque at all. It's just the events which the witness describes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I would suggest that a preliminary question or two might be, What do you know about the situation in other parts of the territory and how do you know it before we hear an expansion on whatever he might want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps I was wrong in assuming that that would have been implicit in Mr. Zecevic's question. But perhaps Mr. Hannis is formally correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree. And I'm grateful to Mr. Hannis for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you heard the question? Are you familiar with the situation in the other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina? And what is your basis for knowing that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I am, in part, familiar with the situation, as it was in the other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. I would like to say something by way of introduction. The operative crime squad of Sarajevo SUP, while carrying out its missions, did not just operate in Sarajevo city area but also throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, depending on the casual links between the various crimes and while identifying and arresting any perpetrators that committed crimes throughout the Sarajevo city. That is why we had a presence in many towns and cities across Bosnia and Herzegovina. We worked closely with a number of other services. There is something that was an open secret, more or less, in Bosnia and Herzegovina and I, too, knew about this. In western Herzegovina, military units had been set up called the Croatian armed forces. I had an occasion to see for myself that indeed these forces were operating. Towards the end of that year, we were work on a case involving a group of perpetrators who were stealing passenger vehicles throughout the Sarajevo city area and then taking the stolen vehicles to Herzegovina. The perpetrators were from the Mostar area, from Listica, from Grude and from Ljubuski. All those are locations in western Herzegovina and the population there is mostly Croatian. Having gathered a certain amount of information and organised this information, we carried on with the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain what you mean by you carried on with the case.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to do that. We had this plan of activities that we were pursuing. So the intention was to take these four municipalities and bring in from the area of these four municipalities a total of five perpetrators, take them to the secretariat of the interior of Sarajevo city in order to conduct interviews with then in order to analyse evidence that was collected against them that would eventually result in a criminal report being submitted to the relevant prosecutor. As for work in the areas of Mostar, Listica, Grude and Ljubuski, two teams were set up for that purpose comprising three inspectors each who had two official vehicles available to them. They drove, first of all, to the Mostar security centre. The head of the local crime police was Jovo Cokorilo. And the head of at centre was an experienced officer, whose name escapes me right now, but he was an ethnic Croat. He warned us that we might encounter incidents happening or that something untoward might happen as we were trying to bring these persons in. He also told us that check-points had been set up along roads leading into these municipalities. These check-points were manned by armed members of the Croatian armed forces. So there were these two teams in official vehicles that first drove to Listica, Siroki Brijeg municipality. As soon as they spotted a check-point along one of the roads, they realised there were members of the Croatian armed forces wearing camouflage uniforms manning those check-points carrying long-barrel automatic weapons. They stopped to observe the check-point, first of all, before driving up to it. As they were doing that, they noticed that those armed men were allowing vehicles with no registration plates to pass through unchecked. Our own vehicles carried Sarajevo plates with the letters SA predominantly displaced. So we took these off, let them in the boot, and we were just waved through. Had they tried to go through the check-point with the plates on, they would have been checked and there probably would have been an incident. They would have been expected to explain why they were on their way to Listica. So the next thing was to bring in this suspect from Listica. This was, if I may call it that, an abridged procedure. The person was located in his home, and the inspectors then brought him in and took him to the Mostar security centre in order to avoid people gathering, blocking their way, making it impossible to bring this person in and take him to Sarajevo. The same day, a similar job was done elsewhere. Again, there were barricades across the road, both in Grude and in Ljubuski. After the person was brought into the premises of the city secretariat of Sarajevo, at some stage I called in the chief of the crime police sector --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was a Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat his name. And go slowly. Let's just make sure that my question is recorded and then we can proceed to your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The name was Rezo Ivo, chief of the crime police sector in the Sarajevo CSB. He was an ethnic Croat. Since we had this action being implemented in a number of municipalities, I called him in, in order to tell him about the case. And on that occasion, after we assessed the intelligence, he agreed that there had been sufficient evidence and indicia to file a criminal complaint. On that same day, an order was issued to keep the person in detention for three days, and then the criminal complaint was forwarded to the relevant prosecutor's office. On that night, we concluded our activities at around 2.00 a.m., and, already at around 6.00 a.m., I received a phone call from Mr. Ivo, Rezo. He was all agitated and told me that he urgently needed information about the activities concerning that case, because there was a lot of pressure coming from the side of the Croatian Democratic Party, HDZ, whose member he was himself. I tried to calm him down, telling him that I could not provide information to a political party and that for anything he needed to know, he should contact Mr. Leutar, my superior. As far as I can recall, I think that under pressure from the HDZ he was soon thereafter removed from office, and as far as I know, he was transferred to Zagreb where he now works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think that you have explained in detail the provenance of what you know. Tell me, do you remember, when was this operation in Herzegovina carried out, this arrest of five perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as for the composition of the team of inspectors who went to arrest the perpetrators in Herzegovina, what was the ethnic background of the inspectors?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: It was a mixed composition. There were members of all three ethnicities: Muslim, Croat, and Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, do you know anything about the situation in Bosanski Brod, and if so, tell us what you know and, again, how you learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I object to relevance. This is not one of our municipalities. I don't know how it furthers our case. I think it is cumulative at best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on a number of occasions, the -- the Office of the Prosecutor insisted on leading evidence which were outside the scope of the indictment, in the territorial sense. And the explanation given was that it shows the -- the widespread, the pattern, the joint criminal enterprise, et cetera. Now, what I'm trying to do with the witness is the very same. I'm trying to counter that position of the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'm trying to show the situation in the overall Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it stood in 1991 and beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. We did seek to lead evidence beyond the scope of the named municipality because it is an element of part of what we charged, that this was a widespread and systematic attack upon civilian populations. However, what Mr. Zecevic is trying to prove is a widespread and systematic tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I expect, Mr. Hannis, that when we come to submissions at the end of the day, this would, no doubt, be a significant plank in the platform on which the Prosecution attacks the evidence for the Defence. However, we have continually had to place the things in their context and I confess I do not, for the moment, and let me emphasise that, see the -- any difficulty with Mr. Zecevic broadening his -- the scope of his questions in the way that he is, in order to -- himself, set the context for their Defence. I am sure that he appreciates that this, any leeway that he has here, should not take all of us down paths which, at the end of the day, are going to lead nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand your point. And maybe it's a matter of quantity. And there's some sort of sliding scale here, but I guess my point is widespread and systematic is something we need to prove and it is contested by the Defence, so it is clearly an issue in this case. Tu quoque, we have not contested that much of what we have alleged was being done by Serbs and the SDS and members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise was also being done by Croatians and the HDZ and by Muslims in the SDA. We haven't contested that. So I don't know how much more of it that you need. I guess that was part of the point that I wanted to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Macar, do you still remember my question?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please answer. Just please be brief, as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I will attempt, but the topics are such that it's hard to put it all into one sentence. And the first thing I would like to say is that our working meetings, given the difficult security situation in town itself, and most of the meetings were held in Mr. Leutar's office, in these meetings, we were informed about the problems in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Already then, in the information that we had in the Ministry of the Interior, and also in the media, it was well-known that the situation in Bosanski Brod was extremely complex, that there were huge ethnic tensions. Paramilitary formations were coming into the area. Those were paramilitary formations of Croatian armed forces. There were also some indication, both from the media and from the material of the Ministry of the Interior, that via the bridge, arms were being smuggled to arm Muslim and Croat forces. In order to resolve the situation and also assist the SJB in Bosanski Brod to establish a more stable security situation, the Ministry of the Interior created a mixed ethnic team, an organisational team, with members from the city SUP of Sarajevo and from the seat of the Ministry of the Interior, and this team was sent to Brod. The team was headed by Avdo Hebib, chief of police, and former psychologist, whom I respect as a good psychologist but not as a good policeman. So he was in charge of the activities, and he was supposed to co-ordinate the work of this team with the work of the local SJB. This team also counted two workers, Skipina, Nenad, who used to work with me in the city SUP, who was an inspector, and also Pekic, Petko, who was my inspector while I still worked in the municipal MUP of Centar municipality. Before the group departed, I had occasion to sit and talk with Skipina. We used to have offices on the same floor, and this is when I learned that he was a member of the that team. While on location there, they took certain measures and they were supposed to secure the border area on the Sava in order to help the SJB in their regular duties; whereas the crime police workers were to help the workers of the crime police in Bosanski Brod police station. After a certain period of time, in early morning hours, Croatian armed forces in the territory -- crossed the Sava from Croatia into Bosanski Brod, and they were assisted by paramilitary formations from Bosanski Brod, and together they took the facility who was normally guarded by people who were on annual leave. What was particularly characteristic, and I learned this from Mr. Skipina, is that Mr. Avdo Hebib did not appear on the day before, even though it was his duty to co-ordinate the work on every day, including that day, and to give -- issue tasks for the following day. After members of the Ministry of the Interior were held up by paramilitaries who had come to Bosanski Brod and who started to harass them, I learned that both inspectors suffered grave mental injury and that they required daily treatment by psychiatrists for the following five to six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Macar, perhaps I should explain to you that, and I bear in mind that, as you said, you have never given evidence before, that when a witness is giving testimony, is something that he might not always appreciate that -- and this is a word that you might hear lawyers use often about relevance, and the reason for that is that, in order to make any trial manageable, it is necessary to confine the evidence that is led to what is determined by, in a criminal case such as this, the indictment. And, therefore, the lawyers who are trained in, among other things, the rules of evidence and procedure, with this in mind, frame their questions in a certain way to invite an answer from the witness because, otherwise, if a witness merely -- were allowed to give a narrative, instinctively because the witness would want to explain why such a such of thing happened, we could find ourselves all the way back in the Garden of Eden. So I would, in this very early stage of your 40-plus hours that you would be with us, ask you to, in the case of counsel for Mr. Stanisic, and, indeed, when it comes to the other side, to listen to the question that counsel asks because counsel has a reason for asking the question that he does and only answer that question. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just two things that need clarification. When you said, on page 38 that Croatian forces, together with paramilitaries from the Bosanski Brod area, took the facility, it was interpreted here that this facility was typically guarded by people who were on annual leave. I think that you said something else, but I hope my learned friend and the Chamber will allow me to focus you on this particular issue. The facility that was occupied, that was taken, was the facility where there were members of the MUP who had come to assist the Bosanski Brod SJB, and those people were led by Avdo Hebib; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, did -- you mentioned the two colleagues of yours. Did you talk to any other members of that team that was sent to Bosanski Brod to assist them there, upon their return? Just briefly. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not talk to them upon their return from Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I only talked to Nenad Skipina and Pekic, Petko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those two blame anyone for being detained by the Croatian forces and paramilitaries in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: They were clear in blaming Mr. Avdo Hebib for not taking up measures to prevent the situation from escalating. One of the measures was supposed to be to cover the border area with Croatia on the Sava river and securing the bridge over Sava with sufficient number of policemen who had been brought to the municipality, precisely for that reason, to assist with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move to early 1992. Do you remember any specific events taking place in Sarajevo which, in your opinion, were relevant for the security situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: What was particularly typical for early 1992, that is to say, January and February, was the complete blocking of the work of municipal organs in the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. When you say "municipal organs," what municipal organs do you have in mind, please?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Primarily municipal secretariat of the interior, in Stari Grad municipality, where police tasks and duties that they were in charge of were not carried out. I also have in mind the police organs in Centar municipality, where parts of the Serb staff members were not included in daily, routine tasks. As for Stari Grad municipality, in several locations there, there were check-points manned by active policemen from the Stari Grad police station, reserve policemen, and Green Berets. That is to say, those were mixed crews. What I saw myself was a check-point in a location just outside of Stari Grad, leading towards Pale, and also near the Stari Grad police station. The constant complaint that arrived to the city secretariat of the interior was that there was a lack of organisation in the police force. The Muslim members tried to include as many Muslim reserve policemen as they could, and through the reserve police forces, they tried to arm them. There was intelligence that the Rijeka neighbourhood, which was populated mostly by people from Sandzak, and where weapons were distributed almost in plain daylight. But nothing was done against that. At some time in 1991, we received intelligence that a truck-load of weapons --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In -- we're in 1992, and my question was about some events that you may be able to single out. I didn't want you to tell us the whole story. We have already heard a lot about it in this trial, but I expected you to mention some crucial events, if any.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Well, there was the murder of a member of the wedding party in early March at Bascarsija. The perpetrator was identified, but nobody from the Stari Grad police station, in whose territory this happened, took anything to apprehend the perpetrator after identification. And what is even more serious, to my mind, is the blockade of the headquarters of the 2nd Army District, which happened on the 15th of March. On that day, in Mr. Leutar's office, we both were informed that the headquarters was blockaded, and due to the ethnic tensions that prevailed in the city, we agreed to go there to see personally what the situation was and to assist the scope of the incident. I think it may have been 11.00 or 12.00 on the 15th of March when we went there. What we witnessed both did and didn't surprise us, with regard to the information about the deviations in the Stari Grad police station. We saw the headquarters surrounded by thousands of citizens. In the first rows, there was Ismet Dahic, the commander of the station; from the MUP, there was Ismet Dautbasic, he was the head of state security; and another executive from the MUP who was in charge of the uniformed police, I forget his name now. Large numbers of police, active and reserve forces with long-barrelled weapons, but they were not protecting the facility from the civilians that had gathered. And in the buildings near the headquarters, or facing the headquarters, there were civilians with weapons, and they didn't even hide. They were very conspicuous. Green Berets were there with Mr. Dahic. I remember the following persons: Ismet Bajramovic, also known as Celo, who even said something vulgar when we were approaching; there was Enko Sakic, a company commander from Bistrik for whom there was a wanted warrant; Enver Svrakic, a Green Berets commander from the city. It was Mr. Leutar who tried to get information directly from Dahic how this had come about, and what the intentions of the police were with a view to preventing further escalation. He mumbled something negative and walked away from us, some 10 metres away, and he didn't want to communicate further. We spent about half an hour there. We returned to the city SUP, where Mr. Leutar briefed his superiors. It was obvious that the police from the municipal secretariat of Stari Grad was not protecting the facility or calming the situation there. Unfortunately, the blockade continued until the tragic incident on Dobrovoljacka Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, all these circumstances you have spoken about since you began testifying, how did they affect the functioning of the MUP, at least as far as the city SUP of Sarajevo was concerned, where you worked? Were there any comments about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Up until the 15th of March or so, we were trying -- I think that we were the only crime police service from Sarajevo who at least tried to go about our security tasks. But since the 15th of March, when communication lines were disrupted between the organisational units of the police, nearly all security work in town stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of the intention to split the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, if so, when, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: In late March 1991, in Mr. Leutar's office, I learned that the Croats, due to the recent developments and the newly created situation, had already established their own police headquarters in Mostar and that some staff had already gone there. Then -- and also that they were active about equipping that institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. It was said here in late March 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Actually, it was 1992, I think. I misspoke. It was 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do continue, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I heard of the establishment of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina round about the 30th of March. Let me add that my daughters, because schools and kindergartens stopped operating --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's drop that now. We'll get there yet. When you were speaking to Mr. Leutar in his office about the establishment of this Croatian MUP in Mostar, what did he say to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: He called me to see him because of the disruption of communication channels and because of the impossibility to do regular policing, and also due to the attempts of the Muslim population to dominate everybody else, for all these reasons the Croatians had decided to set up their own headquarters of the MUP to provide for security in the municipals where the Croats were the majority. And for all these reasons they had decided to establish a Croatian MUP in Herzegovina, its headquarters being in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say to you then what measures had been taken to that effect; and, if so, elaborate, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: He informed me that some Croatian personnel had already gone to personnel and that they were engaged in equipping that ministry with materiel and technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of some attempts from the media, if not otherwise, attempts of the international community to resolve the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I heard about it from the media, and we also learned at working meetings about negotiations. And, finally, there was -- there was agreement reached on the 17th of May or something, about the Cutileiro Plan that envisaged the creation of Ministries of the Interior for all three ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. You said a short while ago, and I interrupted you, that you were aware of the establishment of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in late March. And you were explaining the situation with your daughters. Tell us how you found out about that. Briefly describe the circumstances of that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I was born in Sokolac, as I have said. That's where my parents lived. And because of the security situation in the city of Sarajevo, in mid-March, the schools and kindergartens stopped working. I took my daughters to my parents' house, partly also due to my being so busy, and I didn't want them to be at home alone. And in late March, my wife and I went to see the children and brought them some of things, and so on. And that's when I learned that around the sports complex in Sokolac, on the 30th, there would be a parade of the police of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please play a video-clip to the witness. The reference is 2D1; the transcript of the video material is 1D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Stop here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Macar, did you go to that review in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us who these people are in this still.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: On the right, in a black overcoat, that's me. Next to me there is Milorad Maric, the chief of the Ilijas station, or the SUP of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go to that police troop review in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Well, it was a normal thing to do as a police officer, and as a human being. I wanted to go there and see what was going on, and I was hoping to hear why and how this MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I play you this video-clip so we may see if you remember this part and the speech given at Sokolac on the 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The police force of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija is ready for your review. There are 230 policemen in the lineup, including 70 for carrying out special tasks."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the persons that we see here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stanisic in the overcoat, Zoran Cvijetic in uniform. And the third one is Mr. Krunic, I think. He may have been a member of the Executive Board of Sokolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Zoran Cvijetic, who was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Chief of the Sokolac police station.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The solemn declaration will be read by the minister of the interior of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija, Zoran Cvijetic."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. The presenter introduced him as the minister of the interior of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija, Zoran Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: There were a number of earlier political decisions in Bosnia and Herzegovina by the majority executive authorities, creating autonomous regions which comprised executive bodies, meaning those included representatives of the Ministry of the Interior. In the Romanija-Birac region, it was Zoran Cvijetic who acted as minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we press on with the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I declare that I will perform the duty of authorised official conscientiously and responsibly, that I will abide by the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia and the law, and that I will protect the constitutionally established order of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, rights freedoms and security, and that I will carry out these and other tasks and assignments of authorised officials, even in cases when carrying out these tasks and assignments would bring my life into jeopardy. "The minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mico Stanisic, will address the members of the police unit of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija. "As of today, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has its own police force. Legality of our existence is provided by the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Law on Internal Affairs recently adopted by the Assembly at its session. Moreover, the legality of our existence is based on the result of negotiations of the three ethnic communities under the auspices of the European community. As of today, we will act as the police force of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which will carry out its tasks and assignments professionally and not politically, as the MUP of the old Bosnia-Herzegovina has done so far, in order to protect, property, life, body, and other securities of all citizens in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, equally. "Members of the police, we are not involved in politics. We must carry out our tasks professionally. For these reasons, long speeches do not belong to us. But as of today, good luck. Get to work in the interests of all who live in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, did you recognise this speech and the footage? Were you present there on the 30th of March, 1992, at Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was present for the entire review and also for Mr. Stanisic's speech. I think this speech brought the whole parade to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender both of these, the individual footage, which is D2, and the transcript of Mr. Stanisic's speech, which is D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do we have a tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It wasn't on the original list, but I did get an e-mail indicating that he wanted to add it. I think it's on my list, anyway. And I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm advised by the Court Officer that the transcript is a part of the -- as a part of the documents as one exhibit. So it is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D633, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, on that day, did you meet any of the persons who attended the Sokolac parade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes. Following the parade, I first accosted Mr. Stanisic. I asked him where the ministry HQ would be located and how they will go on establishing the operative functions of the ministry throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I remember, following the speech, Mr. Stanisic told me that the HQ would be at the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that there would be structural talks on the way the work and activities of the ministry would be structured at the BH level and the way work would be co-ordinated. After the parade, I went back to Sarajevo to my office in the Sarajevo city SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, P353 is our next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is tab 4. [In English] I don't see the document on my screen. I don't know whether -- oh, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is a dispatch of the assistant minister of the interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Momcilo Mandic, dated the 31st of March, 1992. Sir, did you see this dispatch on the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I do remember. The 31st of March, there was a meeting in Mr. Leutar's office, it was one of our regular briefings with the department chief, and all the sector heads would be there. He told us about this document, because he had just been to see the secretary, and I see that this is addressed to the secretary of the Sarajevo SUP.
